question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician for a 3-week history of intermittent episodes of dizziness. The episodes last for hours at a time and are characterized by the sensation that the room is spinning. The patient also reports that she has started using her cell phone with her left ear because she hears better on that side. She has experienced intermittent ringing and fullness in her right ear. She has no history of serious medical conditions. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. She takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F) pulse is 76/min respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/76 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. There is horizontal nystagmus to the right. Motor strength is 5/5 in all extremities, and sensory examination shows no abnormalities. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing are normal bilaterally. Weber test shows lateralization to the left ear. The Rinne test is positive bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

options.opb: Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery
options.ope: Obstruction of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Horizontal nystagmus to the right" -> "Weber test lateralization to the left ear" -> "Positive Rinne test bilaterally" -> "Symptoms consistent with peripheral vestibular dysfunction" -> "Possible cause: Reduced resorption of endolymph" -> 70%

CHAIN: "Intermittent episodes of dizziness with room-spinning sensation" -> "Using cell phone with left ear due to hearing better on that side" -> "Intermittent ringing and fullness in right ear" -> "Symptoms suggestive of Meniere's disease" -> "Possible cause: Reduced resorption of endolymph" -> 80%
enhanced_information: The patient's symptoms of intermittent episodes of dizziness with room-spinning sensation, using the cell phone with the left ear, and intermittent ringing and fullness in the right ear are suggestive of Meniere's disease. The findings of horizontal nystagmus to the right, lateralization to the left ear on the Weber test, and positive Rinne test bilaterally support peripheral vestibular dysfunction. The most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is reduced resorption of endolymph, consistent with Meniere's disease.
analysis: The patient's symptoms, examination findings, and enhanced information strongly suggest peripheral vestibular dysfunction, specifically Meniere's disease. The characteristic symptoms of intermittent dizziness, room-spinning sensation, and unilateral hearing loss with tinnitus point towards endolymphatic hydrops. The Weber test lateralizing to the left ear and positive Rinne test bilaterally support this diagnosis.
